name: Electric Motor
tagline: An inductive load that pulls several times its running current to start — protection has to allow for that.
terminals: L and N on a single-phase motor
Start and run windings via the capacitor terminals
parts: Terminal box — where the supply connects
Housing with cooling fins — the stator frame
Capacitor — gives the start (or run) winding its phase shift
Rating plate — volts, amps, power factor, duty
safety: Motors are hard to start and easy to stall: starting current is typically six times the running current, and a stalled motor draws that continuously until the overload trips. Protection must be sized so the motor starts without nuisance tripping while still clearing a stall — and the frame must be earthed. Always isolate, and remember the capacitor can hold a charge after switch-off.

points.label: Terminal box
points.detail: Where the supply lands, usually with a link plate that lets you change the motor between star and delta or reverse its rotation. The lid and its gasket are part of the enclosure rating; the gland must grip the cable, not just the conductors.

points.label: Housing and cooling fins
points.detail: The finned frame is the stator housing and the heat sink. Motors cool by moving air over those fins, so a motor blanketed in dust or boxed in without ventilation runs hot and loses winding life fast.

points.label: Capacitor
points.detail: Single-phase motors have no rotating field of their own; the capacitor shifts the phase of the start (or run) winding to create one. A failed start capacitor leaves the motor humming and not turning — and it stays charged after switch-off, so discharge it before you touch the terminals.

points.label: Drive shaft
points.detail: The output. Couplings and pulleys must be aligned and guarded: a misaligned coupling destroys bearings, and an exposed shaft and keyway is a rotating-entanglement hazard.

points.label: Mounting feet
points.detail: Bolt the motor down solidly and level. A motor that rocks on its feet hammers its own bearings and works the coupling loose; on a resilient mount, make sure the earth bond is not relying on the feet.

points.label: Rating plate
points.detail: Volts, full-load current, power factor, speed, duty and the insulation class. The full-load current is the number you size the cable and the overload from — not the power in watts divided by 230 V, because the power factor is well below one.

cutaway.alt: Cutaway of an electric motor showing the stator windings, rotor cage, shaft, bearings, terminal box and start capacitor

cutawayPoints.label: Stator windings
cutawayPoints.detail: Copper wound into the slots of a laminated steel core. These are what the supply actually feeds, and they are the reason a motor takes several times its running current to start: at standstill there is no back EMF to oppose the supply, so only the winding resistance and leakage reactance limit the current.

cutawayPoints.label: Rotor
cutawayPoints.detail: On an induction motor a cage of aluminium or copper bars joined by end rings at each end — no windings, no brushes, no connection to anything. The rotating stator field induces current in the bars, and that current makes the second field the rotor turns on. The rotor always runs slightly slower than the field, because slip is what induces the current in the first place.

cutawayPoints.label: Drive shaft
cutawayPoints.detail: Carries the torque out through the bearings. It is also the mechanical reference: anything coupled to it has to be aligned, and a shaft running a misaligned load is what destroys the bearings and then the motor.

cutawayPoints.label: Bearings
cutawayPoints.detail: The wearing parts, and the ones that tell you a motor is dying before it dies: a change in the sound, then heat at the bearing housing, then a seized rotor and a winding that cooks on a stalled supply. Most motor failures reach the windings through the bearings.

cutawayPoints.label: Terminal box
cutawayPoints.detail: Where the supply lands, with links that set star or delta. It is also where the motor rating plate lives, and therefore where you read the full-load current before choosing the cable and the overload — not from the kW stamped on the frame.

cutawayPoints.label: Start or run capacitor
cutawayPoints.detail: Single-phase motors have no rotating field of their own, so a capacitor feeds a second winding out of phase with the first to give the rotor something to turn towards. A failed start capacitor is the classic motor that hums and does not turn: it will sit there drawing locked-rotor current until the protection clears it.
